title: The first split
hookLine: the Sthaviras and the Mahasanghikas part ways; accounts differ on why

cards: Two communities of monks. Both shave their heads, both wear the robe, both recite the Buddha's words and keep a code of discipline.

At some point in the generations after the Buddha, they stop meeting together for the observance day. One side becomes known as the Sthaviras, the elders. The other as the Mahasanghikas, the great community.
Ask why, and you get more than one answer, depending on whose books you open.

teach.b: The Dipavamsa, a chronicle kept in the Theravada tradition, ties the split to Vesali. The monks who lost over the ten points, it says, didn't accept the verdict.
They held a great council of their own and arranged the texts their own way, and from that great assembly came the name Mahasanghika.
Texts preserved in northern traditions, such as a treatise on the schools attributed to Vasumitra, tell it differently.
There the quarrel is over points about the arahant, the fully awakened one: could such a person still have doubts, or not know some things, or need others to tell him he was awakened?
On this telling the split was over what awakening is, not over salt and coins.
Some modern scholars point to yet another text that suggests the elders wanted to add rules to the discipline, and the larger group refused.
If that's right, the side called the great community was the one keeping the old rules unchanged.
None of the three can be checked from outside; the old texts each come from a school with its own memory, and the modern reading rests on one more such text.
The Dipavamsa, from the Sthavira line, remembers its side as keeping faith with Vesali.

The northern treatises remember a quarrel about awakening. You don't have to choose a side to learn from this. The first split teaches a habit: when a story about a division is told, ask who is telling it.

how: Theravada Buddhists trace their lineage through the Sthavira side; East Asian and Tibetan monastic lineages keep Vinaya codes that come from other early schools.

o: monks who left to live as hermits
the elders, one side of the first split

games.q: the first split: tap the pairs.

s: every early source agrees on why the split happened
the Sri Lankan chronicle and northern treatises give different reasons, and modern scholars read yet another text.
one account says the split was over what an arahant can lack
texts kept in northern schools describe a quarrel over whether an awakened one could still have doubts or not know some things.
Mahasanghika means the small breakaway group
the name means the great community.

games.q: in the Sri Lankan chronicle's telling, you're one of the monks whose ten points were rejected at Vesali. what do you do?
o: accept the verdict and give up the ten points.
hold a great council of your own.
games.why: the Dipavamsa says they held their own great council, and the name Mahasanghika comes from it. other accounts give a different cause entirely.

practice: Bring to mind a disagreement you know only from one side, a family rift, a split at work, and tell it to yourself briefly the way you usually hear it.
Then tell it the way the other side might, in their best words, not their worst, and let both versions stand side by side.

wordCard.voice: Sthaviras. The elders' side of the first split, parted from the Mahasanghikas, the great community, for reasons the old accounts don't agree on. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: an elder. in Pali, thera, the root of the name Theravada.

carryVoice: Your line: accounts differ. Each side remembers the split in its own way. Until tomorrow.
